title: Command-Line Arguments and the Environment
summary: What a Linux program finds on its stack at _start - argc, the argv pointers and the zero that ends them, the environment strings after them, walking them in assembly, comparing a string prefix to find a variable such as HOME, turning arguments into numbers, and setting the exit code that scripts check.
markdown:
## The stack at _start

When Linux starts a program, the kernel puts information on the stack before the first instruction runs. At `_start`, `rsp` points at:

| address | holds |
|---|---|
| `[rsp]` | `argc`, the number of arguments (including the program's name) |
| `[rsp + 8]` | `argv[0]`, a pointer to the program's name |
| `[rsp + 16]` | `argv[1]`, the first real argument |
| ... | ... |
| `[rsp + 8 × (argc + 1)]` | 0, the end of `argv` |
| after that | pointers to the environment strings `"NAME=value"`, then 0 |

Each pointer leads to a zero-terminated string. `_start` is not a function (nothing called it), so there is no return address; read these before pushing anything.

## Printing the arguments

```nasm
        global  _start

        section .data
count_msg: db   "arguments: ", 0

        section .text
_start:
        mov     r12, [rsp]              ; argc
        lea     r13, [rsp + 8]          ; &argv[0]

        lea     rdi, [rel count_msg]
        call    print_str
        mov     rdi, r12
        call    print_int
        call    print_newline

        xor     ebx, ebx
.next:  cmp     rbx, r12
        jge     .done
        mov     rdi, rbx
        call    print_int
        mov     edi, ':'
        call    print_char
        mov     edi, ' '
        call    print_char
        mov     rdi, [r13 + rbx*8]      ; argv[i]
        call    print_str
        call    print_newline
        inc     rbx
        jmp     .next
.done:
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

On this site, the Run options let you give arguments; without any, `argc` is 1 and only the program's name is printed. In a terminal, `./program one "two words"` gives `argc` = 3, and the quotes keep `two words` together as one argument.

## The environment

The environment strings start right after the zero that ends `argv`. To find one variable, compare the start of each string with `"NAME="`:

```nasm
        global  _start

        section .data
want:   db      "PATH=", 0
label:  db      "PATH is: ", 0
none:   db      "not set", 0

        section .text
starts_with:                            ; rdi = text, rsi = prefix; rax = 1 if text starts with prefix
.loop:  movzx   eax, byte [rsi]
        test    al, al
        jz      .yes                    ; reached the end of the prefix
        cmp     al, [rdi]
        jne     .no
        inc     rdi
        inc     rsi
        jmp     .loop
.yes:   mov     eax, 1
        ret
.no:    xor     eax, eax
        ret

_start:
        mov     rax, [rsp]              ; argc
        lea     rbx, [rsp + 8 + rax*8 + 8]   ; skip argc, the argv pointers and their zero
.scan:  mov     r12, [rbx]
        test    r12, r12
        jz      .missing
        mov     rdi, r12
        lea     rsi, [rel want]
        call    starts_with
        test    eax, eax
        jnz     .found
        add     rbx, 8
        jmp     .scan
.found:
        lea     rdi, [rel label]
        call    print_str
        lea     rdi, [r12 + 5]          ; the value, just after "PATH="
        call    print_str
        call    print_newline
        jmp     .exit
.missing:
        lea     rdi, [rel none]
        call    print_str
        call    print_newline
.exit:  mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

The runner on this site starts programs with an almost empty environment, so the value may be blank here; in a terminal you see your real `PATH`.

The comparison stops at the end of the prefix, so `PATH=` does not match a variable called `PATHEXT=` by accident, because `=` must match too.

## Numbers from arguments

Arguments are always text. Parse them with the same digit loop as lesson 6.02:

```nasm
        global  _start

        section .data
sample: db      "-250", 0

        section .text
parse_int:                              ; rdi = string; rax = value, rdx = 1 if valid
        xor     eax, eax
        xor     ecx, ecx                ; 1 if negative
        cmp     byte [rdi], '-'
        jne     .digits
        mov     ecx, 1
        inc     rdi
.digits:
        movzx   edx, byte [rdi]
        test    dl, dl
        jz      .end
        sub     edx, '0'
        cmp     edx, 9
        ja      .bad                    ; not a digit
        imul    rax, rax, 10
        add     rax, rdx
        inc     rdi
        jmp     .digits
.end:   test    ecx, ecx
        jz      .ok
        neg     rax
.ok:    mov     edx, 1
        ret
.bad:   xor     eax, eax
        xor     edx, edx
        ret

_start:
        lea     rdi, [rel sample]
        call    parse_int
        mov     rdi, rax
        call    print_int               ; -250
        call    print_newline
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

With real arguments, pass `[r13 + 8]` (`argv[1]`) instead of `sample`, after checking that `argc` is at least 2.

## The exit code

The number in `rdi` for the `exit` system call is what the shell sees in `$?`. Scripts depend on it: 0 for success, anything else for failure. A tool that was called wrongly usually prints a short usage message to **standard error** (file descriptor 2) and exits with 2. Run this one here without arguments and the result shows the message and exit code 2:

```nasm
        global  _start

        section .data
usage:  db      "usage: tool NUMBER", 10
usage_len equ   $ - usage

        section .text
_start:
        cmp     qword [rsp], 2          ; argc < 2: no NUMBER given
        jge     .ok
        mov     eax, 1                  ; write(2, usage, usage_len)
        mov     edi, 2
        lea     rsi, [rel usage]
        mov     edx, usage_len
        syscall
        mov     eax, 60
        mov     edi, 2
        syscall
.ok:    mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

## Check yourself
```quiz
? Where is `argv[1]` at `_start`?
- At `[rsp + 8]`
+ At `[rsp + 16]`
- In `rsi`, as in a C `main`
> At `_start`, `[rsp]` is `argc`, `[rsp + 8]` is `argv[0]` and `[rsp + 16]` is `argv[1]`. Registers like `rdi` and `rsi` hold arguments only when a C runtime calls `main`.

? How do you find the first environment pointer?
- It is at `[rsp + 8]`, right after `argc`
+ At `rsp + 8 + argc × 8 + 8`
- At `[rsp + argc × 8]`, after the last `argv` pointer
> Skip `argc`, the `argc` pointers of `argv` and the zero that ends them; the environment pointers come next.

? A program is run as ./tool a b. What is argc?
- 2
+ 3
- 1
- 0
> `argv[0]` is the program's name, so argc counts every word on the command line, the name included.
```
